keep: The stubbornness that isolates you in one decade may be exactly what the next one needs.
lede: By 1940 his career looked like a long record of brilliant failure. Then the catastrophe he had predicted arrived.
copy: A soldier, journalist and politician, he had switched parties twice. He had presided over the Gallipoli disaster. He spent the 1930s in the wilderness, warning about Hitler to an audience that did not want to hear it. Then the very stubbornness that had isolated him became exactly what Britain needed.

As wartime prime minister he refused to negotiate with Nazi Germany when much of the political establishment wanted terms. Through his speeches he gave a frightened nation the language of its own resistance. For a year Britain stood essentially alone. His leadership through it was, by wide agreement, indispensable to the survival of European democracy.

He was also a Victorian imperialist whose views on India and race are rightly condemned, and whose record contains genuine cruelties. The honest reckoning holds both truths: a deeply flawed man who, at the hinge of the twentieth century, was the right person in the right place.

bio.why: Drawing on newly released royal diaries and previously unseen papers, the most comprehensive single-volume life — admiring of 1940 but unsparing about the failures and prejudices.

contested: Roberts is an admirer, and the same author supplies the Napoleon pick on this shelf — worth noticing. On the Bengal famine of 1943 in particular, Madhusree Mukerjee's Churchill's Secret War makes a far harsher case; historians dispute how much causal weight Churchill personally bears. The honest position is that this is actively argued, not settled.
